### 3.2.6 Neurological Examination [^28^]

#### Mental Status
| Component | Assessment | Abnormal Findings |
|-----------|-----------|-------------------|
| **Level of consciousness** | Alert, lethargic, obtunded, stuporous, comatose | Any decrease requires investigation |
| **Orientation** | Person, place, time, situation | Disorientation: delirium, dementia, intoxication |
| **Attention** | Digit span, months backward | Impaired: delirium, intoxication, executive dysfunction |

| **Language** | Fluency, comprehension, repetition, naming | Aphasia: stroke, mass lesion |
| **Executive function** | Clock drawing, serial 7s | Impaired: frontal lobe lesion, dementia |

**Screening Tools:**
| Tool | Score Range | Interpretation | Best For |
|------|------------|---------------|----------|
| **MMSE** | 0-30 | <24: cognitive impairment | General cognitive screening |
| **MoCA** | 0-30 | <26: cognitive impairment | Better sensitivity for MCI |
| **Mini-Cog** | 0-5 | <3: cognitive impairment | Brief screening, language independent |
| **Glasgow Coma Scale** | 3-15 | See Table 3.1.4 | Trauma, acute altered consciousness |

#### Cranial Nerve Examination

| Nerve | Assessment | Abnormal Findings |
|-------|-----------|-------------------|
| **I (Olfactory)** | Smell identification (coffee, vanilla) | Anosmia: head trauma, COVID-19, Parkinson's |
| **II (Optic)** | Visual acuity, fields, fundoscopy | Visual field defects, papilledema |
| **III, IV, VI** | EOMs, pupillary response, ptosis | Diplopia, ptosis (III palsy), strabismus |
| **V (Trigeminal)** | Facial sensation, corneal reflex, jaw strength | Sensory loss, weak masseter |
| **VII (Facial)** | Facial movement symmetry, taste | Facial droop (LMN: Bell's palsy; UMN: stroke) |
| **VIII (Vestibulocochlear)** | Hearing, balance | Sensorineural loss, vertigo |
| **IX, X (Glossopharyngeal, Vagus)** | Gag reflex, palate elevation, voice | Dysphagia, dysarthria, hoarseness |
| **XI (Accessory)** | SCM and trapezius strength | Weakness: neck mass, trauma |
| **XII (Hypoglossal)** | Tongue protrusion symmetry | Deviation toward lesion side |

#### Motor Examination [^29^]

**Tone:**
| Finding | Description | Causes |
|---------|------------|--------|
| Flaccid | Absent resistance | Lower motor neuron lesion, spinal shock, early stroke |
| Normal | Mild resistance to passive movement | |
| Spastic | Velocity-dependent increase in tone | Upper motor neuron lesion (stroke, MS) |
| Rigid | Velocity-independent increase | Parkinson's disease, extrapyramidal |
| Cogwheel | Ratcheting quality | Parkinson's |

**Power — MRC Scale:**
| Grade | Description |
|-------|------------|
| 0 | No contraction |
| 1 | Flicker/trace contraction |
| 2 | Active movement with gravity eliminated |
| 3 | Active movement against gravity |
| 4 | Active movement against some resistance (4-, 4, 4+) |
| 5 | Normal power |

#### Deep Tendon Reflexes

| Reflex | Nerve Root | Technique |
|--------|-----------|-----------|
| Biceps | C5-C6 | Tap biceps tendon with elbow flexed |
| Brachioradialis | C5-C6 | Tap styloid process |
| Triceps | C7-C8 | Tap triceps tendon with arm flexed |
| Patellar | L3-L4 | Tap patellar tendon with leg relaxed |
| Achilles | S1-S2 | Tap Achilles tendon with foot slightly dorsiflexed |

**Grading:**
| Grade | Description |
|-------|------------|
| 0 | Absent |
| 1+ | Diminished |
| 2+ | Normal |
| 3+ | Brisk |
| 4+ | Clonus (pathologic) |

#### Special Signs
| Sign | Maneuver | Positive Indicates |
|------|----------|-------------------|
| **Babinski** | Stroke lateral sole from heel to ball | Upgoing great toe = upper motor neuron lesion |
| **Clonus** | Sudden dorsiflexion of foot | Rhythmic oscillation = hyperreflexia, UMN lesion |
| **Lhermitte** | Passive neck flexion | Electric shock sensation down spine = cervical cord lesion |
| **Hoffmann** | Flick distal phalanx of middle finger | Flexion of thumb/index = UMN lesion |
| **Meningeal signs** | Nuchal rigidity, Kernig, Brudzinski | Meningeal irritation (meningitis, SAH) |

### 3.2.7 Musculoskeletal Examination [^30^] [^31^]

#### Systematic Approach: "Look, Feel, Move"

**Look (Inspection):**
- Symmetry, alignment, deformity
- Muscle bulk (atrophy suggests denervation or disuse)
- Swelling, erythema, ecchymosis, warmth
- Scars, skin changes, wounds

**Feel (Palpation):**
- Point tenderness (localization)
- Warmth (inflammation), crepitus
- Joint effusion (bulge sign, patellar tap)
- Soft tissue masses

**Move:**
| Type | What It Assesses |
|------|-----------------|
| **Active ROM (AROM)** | Patient moves — assesses contractile and non-contractile tissues |
| **Passive ROM (PROM)** | Examiner moves — assesses non-contractile tissues |
| **Resisted testing** | Isometric contraction — assesses tendon and muscle integrity |

#### Musculoskeletal Screening by Region

| Region | Key Screening Maneuvers |
|--------|------------------------|
| **Cervical spine** | Flexion, extension, rotation, lateral bending; Spurling test |
| **Shoulder** | Abduction, external rotation, cross-body adduction; impingement tests |
| **Elbow** | Flexion, extension, supination, pronation |
| **Wrist/Hand** | Grip strength, finger abduction, thumb opposition |
| **Lumbar spine** | Forward flexion (Schober test), extension, lateral bending |
| **Hip** | FABER test, straight leg raise, Thomas test |
| **Knee** | Flexion, extension, Lachman, McMurray, valgus/varus stress |
| **Ankle/Foot** | Dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, inversion, eversion |

## 3.3 Key Clinical Signs and Their Significance

### 3.3.1 Critical Signs Requiring Immediate Action

| Sign | Definition | Associated Conditions | Priority |
|------|-----------|---------------------|----------|
| **Beck's triad** | Hypotension + JVD + muffled heart sounds | Cardiac tamponade | 🚨 |
| **Cushing's triad** | Hypertension + bradycardia + irregular respirations | Increased intracranial pressure | 🚨 |
| **Charcot's triad** | Jaundice + RUQ pain + fever | Ascending cholangitis | 🚨 |
| **Reynolds' pentad** | Charcot's triad + shock + altered mental status | Severe ascending cholangitis | 🚨 |
| **Virchow's triad** | Stasis + hypercoagulability + endothelial injury | Thrombosis (DVT/PE) | ⚠️ |
| **Trousseau sign** | Carpopedal spasm with BP cuff inflation | Hypocalcemia | ⚠️ |
| **Chvostek sign** | Facial twitching with facial nerve tapping | Hypocalcemia | ⚠️ |
| **Murphy sign** | Inspiratory arrest with RUQ palpation | Acute cholecystitis | ⚠️ |
| **McBurney point tenderness** | Tenderness 2/3 umbilicus to ASIS | Appendicitis | ⚠️ |
| **Obturator sign** | Pain with internal rotation of flexed hip | Pelvic abscess/appendicitis | ⚠️ |
| **Kernig sign** | Pain with knee extension while hip flexed | Meningeal irritation | ⚠️ |
| **Brudzinski sign** | Hip flexion with passive neck flexion | Meningeal irritation | ⚠️ |

### 3.3.2 Common Clinical Signs by System

| Sign | Description | Significance |
|------|------------|-------------|
| **Clubbing** | Increased nail bed angle (>180°), loss of Lovibond angle | Chronic hypoxia: lung cancer, CF, bronchiectasis, cyanotic heart disease, IBD |
| **Splinter hemorrhages** | Linear brown-black streaks under nails | Endocarditis, trauma, vasculitis |
| **Janeway lesions** | Painless erythematous macules on palms/soles | Infective endocarditis (embolic) |
| **Osler nodes** | Painful nodules on fingers/toes | Infective endocarditis (immune complex) |
| **Roth spots** | Retinal hemorrhages with pale centers | Endocarditis, leukemia, vasculitis |
| **Spider angiomas** | Central arteriole with radiating vessels | Liver disease, pregnancy, estrogen excess |
| **Palmar erythema** | Reddening of thenar/hypothenar eminences | Liver disease, pregnancy, hyperthyroidism |
| **Caput medusae** | Dilated periumbilical veins | Portal hypertension |
| **Asterixis** | Flapping tremor with wrist extension | Hepatic encephalopathy, uremia, hypercapnia |
| **Cullen sign** | Periumbilical ecchymosis | Retroperitoneal hemorrhage (pancreatitis, ruptured AAA) |
| **Grey Turner sign** | Flank ecchymosis | Retroperitoneal hemorrhage |
| **Virchow node** | Left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy | Metastatic abdominal malignancy (Troisier sign) |
| **Horner syndrome** | Ptosis + miosis + anhidrosis | Pancoast tumor, carotid dissection, lateral medullary syndrome |
| **Homans sign** | Calf pain with dorsiflexion | Unreliable for DVT diagnosis |

## 3.4 Documentation Standards

### 3.4.1 SOAP Note Format

The SOAP format provides a structured approach to clinical documentation:

| Section | Content |
|---------|---------|
| **S (Subjective)** | Chief complaint; HPI (including OPQRST); ROS; PMH; PSH; FH; SH; Allergies; Medications |
| **O (Objective)** | Vital signs; Physical examination findings; Lab results; Imaging results |
| **A (Assessment)** | Differential diagnosis with most likely first; Clinical reasoning |
| **P (Plan)** | Diagnostic tests ordered; Medications prescribed; Procedures performed; Patient education; Follow-up plan; Return precautions |

### 3.4.2 Documentation Best Practices

| Principle | Application |
|-----------|------------|
| **Timeliness** | Document during or immediately after the encounter |
| **Completeness** | Include all relevant positive and negative findings |
| **Accuracy** | Record objective data; use quotations for patient statements |
| **Legibility** | Use clear, standard terminology and abbreviations |
| **Organization** | Use consistent format; group related findings |
| **Attribution** | Identify source of information (patient, family, records) |
| **Revisions** | Clearly mark addenda with date, time, and reason |

### 3.4.3 Red Flag Documentation

Always prominently document:
- Abnormal vital signs with trend
- Safety concerns (suicidal ideation, abuse) and actions taken
- Decisions to deviate from standard care and rationale
- Informed consent discussions
- Patient refusal of recommended care
- Follow-up instructions and return precautions
- Communication with other providers

### 3.4.4 Physical Exam Documentation Templates

**General Template:**
```
GENERAL: [Alert/oriented x3, NAD, mild distress, etc.]
VITALS: [T, HR, BP, RR, SpO2, Pain, Weight]
HEENT: [Head normocephalic; PERRLA; EOMI; TMs clear; Oropharynx clear]
NECK: [Supple, no JVD, no LAD, thyroid normal]
CARDIOVASCULAR: [RRR, no m/r/g; distal pulses 2+ bilaterally]
RESPIRATORY: [CTA bilaterally, no w/r/r]
ABDOMEN: [Soft, NT, ND, +BS, no HSM]
EXTREMITIES: [No c/c/e; warm, well-perfused]
NEURO: [CN II-XII intact; strength 5/5 all extremities; sensation intact; gait normal]
SKIN: [Warm, dry, no rashes or lesions]
PSYCH: [Appropriate affect, mood normal, no SI/HI]
```

# Chapter 4: Diagnostic Reasoning

## Overview

Diagnostic reasoning is the cognitive process by which clinicians synthesize clinical information to arrive at accurate diagnoses and appropriate management plans. Despite advances in technology, diagnostic error remains a significant patient safety concern, affecting an estimated 10-15% of diagnoses. This chapter provides frameworks for systematic diagnostic reasoning, evidence-based use of clinical prediction rules, rational interpretation of diagnostic tests, and awareness of cognitive biases that can lead to error. [^32^] [^33^] [^34^]

**Key Principle:** *Good diagnostic reasoning is both an art and a science — it requires systematic application of clinical epidemiology combined with careful attention to the cognitive processes underlying clinical judgment.*

---

## 4.1 Bayesian Reasoning Framework

### 4.1.1 Core Principle

Bayesian reasoning provides the mathematical foundation for clinical diagnosis. It describes how the probability of a disease changes in response to new clinical information. Every piece of clinical data — from the patient's age and risk factors to physical examination findings and test results — updates the probability of disease. [^35^]

**Bayes' Theorem (Odds Form):**

> Post-test Odds = Pre-test Odds × Likelihood Ratio

This simple equation underlies all diagnostic testing decisions.

### 4.1.2 Pre-Test Probability

Pre-test probability is the probability of disease before performing a diagnostic test. It integrates:

| Source of Information | Examples |
|----------------------|----------|
| **Population prevalence** | Age-adjusted disease rates, screening data |
| **Patient history** | Risk factors, exposures, prior disease |
| **Clinical presentation** | Symptom patterns, duration, severity |
| **Physical examination** | Specific signs with known diagnostic value |
| **Previous test results** | Prior laboratory or imaging findings |

**Why Pre-Test Probability Matters:** [^35^]

1. **A positive test in a low-prevalence setting** has lower positive predictive value (more false positives)
2. **A negative test in a high-prevalence setting** has lower negative predictive value (more false negatives)
3. **Tests have greatest utility at intermediate pre-test probabilities** where results change clinical management
4. **Sequential testing** uses the post-test probability from one test as the pre-test probability for the next

### 4.1.3 Practical Application: A Worked Example

**Clinical Scenario:** A 55-year-old man with hypertension and dyslipidemia presents with exertional chest pressure. His pre-test probability of coronary artery disease based on age, sex, and symptoms is approximately 30%.

**Exercise ECG Test Characteristics:**
- Sensitivity = 70%
- Specificity = 85%
- LR(+) = 0.70 / (1 - 0.85) = 4.67
- LR(-) = (1 - 0.70) / 0.85 = 0.35

**If exercise ECG is POSITIVE:**
- Pre-test odds = 0.30 / 0.70 = 0.43
- Post-test odds = 0.43 × 4.67 = 2.0
- Post-test probability = 2.0 / (2.0 + 1) = **67%**

**If exercise ECG is NEGATIVE:**
- Pre-test odds = 0.30 / 0.70 = 0.43
- Post-test odds = 0.43 × 0.35 = 0.15
- Post-test probability = 0.15 / (0.15 + 1) = **13%**

**Clinical Decision:** A positive test raises probability to 67%, warranting coronary angiography. A negative test reduces probability to 13%, suggesting medical management with risk factor modification may be appropriate.

### 4.1.4 Threshold Approach to Testing

| Threshold | Probability Range | Action |
|-----------|------------------|--------|
| **Testing threshold** | Below testing threshold | No testing needed; clinical follow-up |
| **Test range** | Between testing and treatment thresholds | Perform diagnostic test |
| **Treatment threshold** | Above treatment threshold | Treat without further testing |

**Example — PE Testing Thresholds:**
- Wells score ≤4: PE unlikely → D-dimer testing (testing threshold)
- Wells score >4: PE likely → Skip D-dimer, proceed to CTPA (above testing threshold)
- High-probability PE with hemodynamic instability: Treat empirically (above treatment threshold)

---

## 4.2 Differential Diagnosis Methodology

### 4.2.1 Framework for Differential Diagnosis

A systematic approach to differential diagnosis ensures life-threatening conditions are considered first and no important diagnosis is overlooked.

#### VINDICATE Mnemonic (Comprehensive)

| Letter | Category | Examples |
|--------|----------|----------|
| **V** | Vascular | MI, PE, stroke, aortic dissection, mesenteric ischemia |
| **I** | Inflammatory/Infectious | Pneumonia, meningitis, endocarditis, autoimmune disease |
| **N** | Neoplastic | Lung cancer, colon cancer, lymphoma, brain tumor |
| **D** | Degenerative/Deficiency | Osteoarthritis, dementia, vitamin B12 deficiency |
| **I** | Iatrogenic/Idiopathic | Drug side effects, medication interactions |
| **C** | Congenital | Structural heart disease, hereditary conditions |
| **A** | Autoimmune/Allergic | Lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, anaphylaxis |
| **T** | Traumatic/Toxic | Fractures, concussion, overdose, environmental exposure |
| **E** | Endocrine/Environmental | Thyroid disease, diabetes, adrenal crisis, heat stroke |

#### Prioritization Framework

| Priority | Category | Rationale |
|----------|----------|-----------|
| **First** | Life-threatening conditions ("must not miss") | Patient safety imperative; time-sensitive treatment |
| **Second** | Common conditions | "When you hear hoofbeats, think horses, not zebras" |
| **Third** | Treatable conditions | Earlier diagnosis improves outcomes |
| **Fourth** | Chronic/degenerative conditions | Important for management but not emergent |

### 4.2.2 Problem Representation (One-Liner Summary)

Problem representation is a concise summary of the case that facilitates clinical reasoning and communication:

**Format:**
> [Patient demographic] with [relevant history] presents with [duration] of [symptom] characterized by [key features], associated with [relevant positives], without [relevant negatives].

**Example:**
> "65-year-old male with 40 pack-year smoking history and COPD presents with 3 days of progressive dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, associated with fever and tachycardia, without hemoptysis or unilateral leg swelling."

### 4.2.3 Illness Scripts

Illness scripts are mental models that integrate disease knowledge with clinical experience. They include:

| Component | Content |
|-----------|---------|
| **Pre-conditions** | Risk factors, patient characteristics, setting |
| **Fault** | Pathophysiologic mechanism |
| **Clinical consequences** | Symptoms, signs, typical presentation |
| **Management** | Standard treatment and expected response |

Experienced clinicians develop richer, more nuanced illness scripts through repeated exposure to typical and atypical presentations.

---

## 4.3 Clinical Prediction Rules

### 4.3.1 Overview

Clinical prediction rules (CPRs) combine clinical variables to estimate probability or predict outcomes. They reduce variability, improve diagnostic accuracy, and guide resource utilization when properly validated and applied. [^36^]

### 4.3.2 Key Clinical Prediction Rules in Primary Care

| Rule | Purpose | Components | Interpretation |
|------|---------|-----------|---------------|
| **Wells Score (PE)** | PE pre-test probability | Clinical signs of DVT (3), PE most likely dx (3), HR>100 (1.5), immobilization (1.5), prior PE/DVT (1.5), hemoptysis (1), malignancy (1) | >4: likely PE; ≤4: unlikely PE |
| **Revised Geneva Score** | PE pre-test probability | Age >65 (1), prior DVT/PE (3), surgery/fracture (2), active malignancy (2), unilateral leg pain (3), hemoptysis (2), HR 95-110 (1) or >110 (2), pain on palpation (3) | 0-3: low; 4-10: intermediate; ≥11: high |
| **HEART Score** | ACS risk stratification | History (0-2), ECG (0-2), Age (0-2), Risk factors (0-2), Troponin (0-2) | 0-3: low risk; 4-6: moderate; 7-10: high |
| **CURB-65** | Pneumonia severity | Confusion (1), Urea >7 mmol/L (1), RR ≥30 (1), BP <90/60 (1), Age ≥65 (1) | 0-1: outpatient; 2: short hospitalization; ≥3: severe, ICU |
| **CHA2DS2-VASc** | Stroke risk in AF | CHF (1), HTN (1), Age ≥75 (2), Diabetes (1), Stroke/TIA (2), Vascular disease (1), Age 65-74 (1), Female (1) | ≥2 (men) or ≥3 (women): anticoagulation indicated |
| **HAS-BLED** | Bleeding risk on anticoagulation | HTN (1), Abnormal renal/hepatic function (1-2), Stroke (1), Bleeding history (1), Labile INR (1), Elderly >65 (1), Drugs/alcohol (1-2) | ≥3: high bleeding risk — closer monitoring |
| **Wells Score (DVT)** | DVT probability | Active cancer (1), paralysis/immobilization (1), bedridden >3 days (1), localized tenderness (1), swollen leg (1), calf swelling >3 cm (1), pitting edema (1), collateral veins (1), alternative diagnosis (-2) | ≥2: DVT likely; <2: DVT unlikely |

### 4.3.3 Clinical Prediction Rule Application Principles

| Principle | Implementation |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Validate in your population** | CPRs developed in one setting may not perform identically in another |
| **Apply to appropriate patients** | Do not apply CPRs outside the population in which they were validated |
| **Use as adjunct, not replacement** | CPRs support but do not replace clinical judgment |
| **Consider spectrum bias** | Performance may vary in different clinical settings |
| **Understand limitations** | No CPR is perfect; false positives and negatives occur |

---

## 4.4 Diagnostic Testing Interpretation

### 4.4.1 Sensitivity and Specificity

| Parameter | Definition | Formula | Clinical Application |
|-----------|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| **Sensitivity (Sn)** | Probability of positive test given disease present | TP / (TP + FN) | RULE OUT: High SnNOut |
| **Specificity (Sp)** | Probability of negative test given disease absent | TN / (TN + FP) | RULE IN: High SpPIn |
| **Positive Predictive Value (PPV)** | Probability of disease given positive test | TP / (TP + FP) | Depends on prevalence |
| **Negative Predictive Value (NPV)** | Probability of no disease given negative test | TN / (TN + FN) | Depends on prevalence |

**Key Relationships:**
- Sensitivity and specificity are **inversely related** through the test cutoff threshold
- Raising the cutoff: ↑ specificity, ↓ sensitivity
- Lowering the cutoff: ↑ sensitivity, ↓ specificity
- PPV and NPV **depend on disease prevalence** — they change with the population tested

**Clinical Application — SnNOut and SpPIn:**

| Mnemonic | Meaning | Application |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| **SnNOut** | **S**ensitive test, **N**egative result rules **Out** disease | Screening tests (HIV screening, D-dimer for PE) |
| **SpPIn** | **S**pecific test, **P**ositive result rules **In** disease | Confirmatory tests (CTPA for PE, Western blot for HIV) |

### 4.4.2 Likelihood Ratios [^35^] [^37^]

Likelihood ratios are the preferred measures for diagnostic test interpretation because they remain constant across different disease prevalences.

| Calculation | Formula |
|-------------|---------|
| **LR(+)** | Sensitivity / (1 - Specificity) = How much a positive test increases disease odds |
| **LR(-)** | (1 - Sensitivity) / Specificity = How much a negative test decreases disease odds |

**Interpretation Scale:**

| LR Value | Interpretation | Impact on Probability |
|----------|---------------|----------------------|
| >10 | Excellent positive test | Large increase |
| 5-10 | Good positive test | Moderate increase |
| 2-5 | Fair positive test | Small increase |
| 1-2 | Poor positive test | Minimal change |
| 0.5-1 | Poor negative test | Minimal decrease |
| 0.2-0.5 | Fair negative test | Small decrease |
| 0.1-0.2 | Good negative test | Moderate decrease |
| <0.1 | Excellent negative test | Large decrease |

**Practical Application:** LR(+) >10 or LR(-) <0.1 generally results in probability changes large enough to change clinical management.

### 4.4.3 Fagan Nomogram

The Fagan Nomogram is a graphical tool to convert pre-test probability to post-test probability:

1. Identify pre-test probability on the left axis
2. Draw a straight line through the LR value on the middle axis
3. Read the post-test probability where the line intersects the right axis

This visual tool helps clinicians understand the clinical impact of test results without calculation.

### 4.4.4 Common Primary Care Tests: Characteristics

| Test | Condition | Sensitivity | Specificity | LR(+) | LR(-) |
|------|-----------|-------------|-------------|-------|-------|
| **Troponin I** (high-sensitivity) | Acute MI | ~95% | ~95% | 19 | 0.05 |
| **D-dimer** | PE/DVT | ~95% | ~45% | 1.7 | 0.11 |
| **Chest X-ray** | Pneumonia | ~70% | ~90% | 7 | 0.33 |
| **Rapid strep test** | Strep pharyngitis | ~85% | ~95% | 17 | 0.16 |
| **Urine dipstick (leuk est)** | UTI | ~75% | ~70% | 2.5 | 0.36 |
| **Hemoglobin A1c ≥6.5%** | Diabetes | ~50% | ~95% | 10 | 0.53 |

### 4.4.5 Common Diagnostic Testing Pitfalls

| Pitfall | Description | Prevention |
|---------|-------------|-----------|
| **Ordering tests before forming a differential** | "Shotgun" testing leads to false positives | Formulate differential first; test discriminating features |
| **Ignoring pre-test probability** | Positive D-dimer in low-probability PE | Apply clinical prediction rules before testing |
| **Ordering tests that won't change management** | A1c screening in terminal cancer patient | Ask "Will this result change what I do?" |
| **Failing to repeat borderline tests** | Single slightly elevated TSH | Confirm abnormalities before acting |
| **Ordering tests inappropriately** | CT scan for uncomplicated headache | Follow Choosing Wisely recommendations |

## 4.5 Cognitive Bias Awareness

### 4.5.1 Dual-Process Theory [^33^]

Clinical reasoning operates through two cognitive systems:

| Feature | System 1 (Fast/Intuitive) | System 2 (Slow/Analytical) |
|---------|--------------------------|---------------------------|
| **Speed** | Automatic, rapid | Deliberate, slow |
| **Effort** | Low cognitive load | High cognitive effort |
| **Mechanism** | Pattern recognition, heuristics, intuition | Rule-based, methodical, analytical |
| **Accuracy** | High for common, typical presentations | Higher for complex, atypical presentations |
| **Vulnerability** | Prone to cognitive biases | More resistant but not immune |
| **Best use** | Common, straightforward cases | Complex, high-stakes, atypical cases |

**Clinical Reality:** Experienced clinicians use System 1 for most routine cases but must recognize when to engage System 2 for complex or atypical presentations.

### 4.5.2 Common Cognitive Biases in Diagnosis [^32^] [^33^] [^34^]

| Bias | Definition | Clinical Example | Mitigation Strategy |
|------|-----------|-----------------|-------------------|
| **Anchoring** | Fixating on initial information or diagnosis | Accepting "heartburn" diagnosis for chest pain without considering ACS | Actively consider alternatives; revisit all data |
| **Availability** | Judging likelihood by ease of recent recall | Diagnosing PE because you just saw a PE case | Consider base rates; systematic differential |
| **Confirmation bias** | Seeking data to confirm rather than refute | Ordering tests to support your preferred diagnosis | Actively seek disconfirming evidence |
| **Premature closure** | Accepting a diagnosis before fully exploring | Diagnosing anxiety for tachycardia without checking TSH | Generate complete differential before finalizing |
| **Representativeness** | Judging by similarity to prototype | Missing atypical MI presentation in young woman | Consider atypical presentations in all patients |
| **Attribution bias** | Blaming patient characteristics (psychosomatic) | Attributing abdominal pain in anxious patient to stress | Maintain diagnostic humility; complete workup |
| **Overconfidence** | Overestimating accuracy of own judgment | Not seeking consultation when uncertain | Use checklists; seek second opinions |
| **Sunk cost** | Continuing a path due to prior investment | Continuing antibiotic for "pneumonia" not improving on imaging | Reassess when not responding to treatment |
| **Framing effect** | Decision influenced by information presentation | Accepting treatment described as "90% survival" vs. "10% mortality" | Consider data from multiple perspectives |
| **Search satisficing** | Stopping after finding first abnormality | Finding gallstones on CT and missing coexistent mass | Complete full systematic evaluation |

### 4.5.3 Impact of Cognitive Biases

Research demonstrates that cognitive biases are associated with diagnostic errors in up to **77%** of case studies. Anchoring bias is the most prominent cognitive bias in non-concordant diagnoses. [^33^]

| Error Type | Frequency | Primary Contributing Biases |
|-----------|-----------|---------------------------|
| Missed diagnosis | ~40% | Premature closure, availability, framing |
| Wrong diagnosis | ~30% | Anchoring, confirmation, overconfidence |
| Delayed diagnosis | ~30% | Attribution, sunk cost, search satisficing |

### 4.5.4 Debiasing Strategies

| Strategy | Implementation |
|----------|---------------|
| **Metacognition** | "Think about your thinking" — pause to consider your reasoning process |
| **Consider the opposite** | Actively seek evidence against your leading diagnosis |
| **Systematic checklists** | Use structured differentials and checklists |
| **Second opinions** | Fresh perspective on complex or unusual cases |
| **Deliberate reflection** | Take time before finalizing diagnosis |
| **Reference to base rates** | Consider disease prevalence in your population |
| **Probabilistic reasoning** | Quantify pre-test probability explicitly |
| **Cognitive forcing strategies** | Require consideration of alternatives before committing |

### 4.5.5 Diagnostic Safety Checklist

Before finalizing any diagnosis, verify:

1. [ ] Have I considered all life-threatening possibilities?
2. [ ] Does the presentation fit the timeline of my leading diagnosis?
3. [ ] Have I sought disconfirming evidence for my leading diagnosis?
4. [ ] Have I explained ALL of the patient's findings?
5. [ ] Does the patient have risk factors for alternative diagnoses?
6. [ ] Would a colleague agree with my reasoning?
7. [ ] Have I documented my reasoning?
8. [ ] Do I have a follow-up plan to reassess if not improving?

# Chapter 5: Evidence-Based Medicine Principles

## Overview

Evidence-based medicine (EBM) is the conscientious, explicit, and judicious use of current best evidence in making decisions about the care of individual patients. It integrates clinical expertise with the best available external evidence and patient values. This chapter covers the evidence hierarchy, the GRADE system, practical calculations for number needed to treat and harm, shared decision-making frameworks, and strategies for applying population-level guidelines to individual patients. [^38^] [^39^] [^40^]

**Core Principle:** *Evidence informs but does not dictate clinical decisions. The best evidence must always be integrated with clinical judgment and patient preferences.*

---

## 5.1 Evidence Hierarchy and GRADE System

### 5.1.1 Levels of Evidence Hierarchy

Evidence hierarchies rank study designs by their ability to minimize bias and provide reliable estimates of treatment effects.

#### Oxford/Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine Levels [^38^]

| Level | Description | Reliability |
|-------|-------------|------------|
| **1A** | Systematic review (with homogeneity) of RCTs | Highest — consistent findings across multiple high-quality studies |
| **1B** | Individual RCT (narrow confidence intervals) | High — single well-designed study |
| **1C** | All-or-none study | High — dramatic treatment effect when no treatment existed |
| **2A** | Systematic review (homogeneity) of cohort studies | Moderate-High — consistent observational evidence |
| **2B** | Individual cohort study (including low-quality RCT) | Moderate — observational data with inherent biases |
| **2C** | "Outcomes" research; ecological studies | Lower — population-level correlations |
| **3A** | Systematic review of case-control studies | Moderate — retrospective comparisons |
| **3B** | Individual case-control study | Lower — prone to recall and selection bias |
| **4** | Case series and poor quality cohort/case-control | Low — no comparison group |
| **5** | Expert opinion without explicit critical appraisal | Lowest — based on physiology or unsystematic clinical experience |

**Hierarchy of Study Designs for Different Clinical Questions:**

| Clinical Question | Preferred Study Design | Alternative |
|-------------------|----------------------|-------------|
| **Therapy/Prevention** | RCT > Cohort > Case-control | Systematic review of RCTs preferred |
| **Diagnosis** | Cross-sectional study with consecutive patients | Systematic review of diagnostic accuracy studies |
| **Prognosis** | Prospective cohort study | Systematic review of cohort studies |
| **Harm/Etiology** | Cohort > Case-control > RCT | Often RCTs are unethical for harm studies |
| **Economic analysis** | Cost-effectiveness analysis alongside RCT | Decision modeling |

### 5.1.2 GRADE System [^39^]

The GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) system is the most widely used framework for rating quality of evidence and strength of recommendations.

#### Starting Point for Evidence Quality

| Study Type | Starting Quality |
|------------|-----------------|
| **Randomized controlled trials** | High |
| **Observational studies** | Low |

#### Factors that DECREASE Evidence Quality (Rate Down)

| Factor | Description | Potential Downgrade |
|--------|-------------|-------------------|
| **Limitations in study design** | Risk of bias — inadequate randomization, lack of blinding, high attrition | 1-2 levels |
| **Inconsistency** | Heterogeneity of results across studies — varying effect sizes, direction of effect | 1-2 levels |
| **Indirectness** | Differences between study population and target population; different interventions or outcomes | 1-2 levels |
| **Imprecision** | Wide confidence intervals; small sample size; few events | 1-2 levels |
| **Publication bias** | Selective publication of positive results; industry funding | 1-2 levels |

#### Factors that INCREASE Evidence Quality (Rate Up)

| Factor | Description | Potential Upgrade |
|--------|-------------|------------------|
| **Large magnitude of effect** | Very large treatment effect (RR >2 or <0.5) | 1-2 levels |
| **Plausible confounding would reduce effect** | If residual confounding likely works against the observed effect | 1 level |
| **Dose-response gradient** | Greater effect with higher dose or exposure | 1 level |

#### Final GRADE Quality Categories

| Category | Definition | Implication |
|----------|-----------|-------------|
| **High** | Further research is very unlikely to change confidence in the effect estimate | Strong recommendations can be made |
| **Moderate** | Further research is likely to have an important impact on confidence | Moderate strength recommendations |
| **Low** | Further research is very likely to have an important impact | Weak/conditional recommendations |
| **Very Low** | Any estimate of effect is very uncertain | Recommendations based on expert opinion |

### 5.1.3 2024 ESC Revised Evidence Grading [^40^]

The European Society of Cardiology has adopted a revised evidence grading system:

| Level | Definition |
|-------|-----------|
| **A** | Conclusive evidence from ≥2 adequately powered RCTs with substantial evidence against play of chance |
| **B1** | Suggestive evidence from ≥1 adequately powered RCT with some evidence against play of chance |
| **B2** | Limited evidence from ≥2 adequately powered non-randomized studies with careful bias control |
| **C** | Preliminary evidence from non-randomized studies without careful bias control, small RCTs, or expert consensus |

#### Class of Recommendation (COR)

| Class | Definition | Wording |
|-------|-----------|---------|
| **I** | Evidence and/or general agreement that treatment is beneficial/useful/effective | "Is recommended" |
| **IIa** | Weight of evidence/opinion is in favor of usefulness/efficacy | "Is reasonable" |
| **IIb** | Usefulness/efficacy is less well established | "May be considered" |
| **III (no benefit)** | Evidence that intervention is not useful/effective AND may be harmful | "Is not recommended" |
| **III (harm)** | Evidence that intervention is harmful | "Should not be done" |

### 5.1.4 Applying Evidence Hierarchy in Practice

| Scenario | Evidence Level | Recommendation Strength |
|----------|---------------|------------------------|
| Statin therapy for secondary CVD prevention | High (multiple large RCTs) | Strong (Class I) |
| Aspirin for primary prevention in low-risk adults | Moderate (updated data showing limited benefit, bleeding risk) | Weak (Class IIb/III) |
| Anticoagulation for AF (CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2) | High (multiple RCTs) | Strong (Class I) |
| Exercise for depression | Moderate (RCTs with methodological limitations) | Moderate |
| Probiotics for antibiotic-associated diarrhea | Low (heterogeneous studies, varying strains) | Weak |

## 5.2 NNT/NNH Calculations

### 5.2.1 Definitions

| Metric | Definition | Clinical Meaning |
|--------|-----------|-----------------|
| **NNT (Number Needed to Treat)** | Average number of patients who need to be treated to prevent one additional adverse outcome | Lower NNT = more effective treatment |
| **NNH (Number Needed to Harm)** | Average number of patients who need to be exposed to cause one additional adverse outcome | Higher NNH = safer treatment |
| **NNT/NNH Ratio** | Balance of benefit vs. harm | Helps assess net clinical benefit |

### 5.2.2 Calculation Method [^41^] [^42^]

**Step 1: Calculate Absolute Risk Reduction (ARR)**

> ARR = Control Event Rate (CER) - Experimental Event Rate (EER)

**Step 2: Calculate NNT**

> NNT = 1 / ARR

**Worked Example:** [^42^]
- Drug reduces MI risk from 4% to 2%
- CER = 0.04; EER = 0.02
- ARR = 0.04 - 0.02 = 0.02
- NNT = 1 / 0.02 = **50**
- **Interpretation:** 50 patients need to be treated for the specified duration to prevent 1 MI

**For NNH:**
- NNH = 1 / Absolute Risk Increase (ARI)
- ARI = EER - CER (when experimental rate is worse)

### 5.2.3 NNT for Time-to-Event Outcomes [^41^]

At a specific time point:

> NNT(t) = 1 / |S_control(t) - S_treatment(t)|

Where S = survival probability

**Example:** If 5-year survival is 80% with treatment and 70% without:
- NNT(5 years) = 1 / |0.80 - 0.70| = 1 / 0.10 = **10**
- Interpretation: 10 patients need treatment for 5 years to prevent 1 death

### 5.2.4 Practical Considerations [^41^]

| Consideration | Application |
|--------------|-------------|
| **Always specify time frame** | "NNT = 4 to prevent one case of PONV within 24 hours" |
| **Confidence intervals** | If 95% CI includes infinity, result is not statistically significant |
| **Baseline risk matters** | Same relative effect yields different NNT in high vs. low-risk populations |
| **Do not pool NNTs directly** | Pool absolute risk reductions first, then compute NNT |
| **Patient characteristics** | Use NNT from studies matching your patient's risk profile |
| **NNT varies with outcome** | One treatment may have different NNTs for different outcomes |

### 5.2.5 Common NNT Examples in Primary Care [^42^]

| Intervention | Population | Outcome | NNT | Timeframe |
|-------------|-----------|---------|-----|-----------|
| **Statins** | High-risk CVD | Prevent major CV event | ~20-50 | 5 years |
| **Aspirin** | Low-risk adults | Prevent MI | ~250 | 5 years |
| **Metformin** | Prediabetes | Prevent progression to diabetes | ~4 | 3 years |
| **Antihypertensives** | Moderate risk | Prevent stroke | ~50-100 | 5 years |
| **Smoking cessation** | Smokers | Prevent death | ~20-50 | Lifetime |
| **Influenza vaccine** | Adults 65+ | Prevent hospitalization | ~30-40 | 1 season |
| **Falls prevention** | Community elderly | Prevent one fall | ~10 | 1 year |

### 5.2.6 Limitations of NNT/NNH [^43^] [^44^]

| Limitation | Explanation |
|-----------|-------------|
| **Comparison-specific** | NNT compares two treatments, not a single intervention vs. nothing |
| **Baseline risk dependent** | Derived from specific study populations |
| **Time-dependent** | Changes with duration of follow-up |
| **Does not capture preferences** | Does not incorporate patient values |
| **Confidence interval issues** | Non-significant results yield counterintuitive CIs |
| **Should not be pooled across studies** | Different populations, baselines, and timeframes |

## 5.3 Shared Decision-Making Frameworks

### 5.3.1 Definition and Components

Shared decision-making (SDM) is a collaborative process in which clinicians and patients make healthcare decisions together, combining clinical evidence with patient values and preferences. SDM is particularly important when:

- Multiple reasonable options exist
- Outcomes are uncertain
- Benefits and harms are closely balanced
- Patient values significantly influence the optimal choice

### 5.3.2 Components of Shared Decision-Making

| Step | Clinician Action | Patient Action |
|------|-----------------|---------------|
| **1. Inform** | Provide clear, evidence-based information about options | Listen and ask clarifying questions |
| **2. Present probabilities** | Use natural frequencies and visual aids | Express understanding and concerns |
| **3. Elicit values** | Ask what matters most to the patient | Share personal values and preferences |
| **4. Reach agreement** | Integrate evidence with patient values | Participate actively in the decision |
| **5. Document** | Record the decision-making process | Confirm understanding with teach-back |

### 5.3.3 Communicating Risk Effectively

| Best Practice | Example |
|-------------|---------|
| **Use absolute risks, not just relative risks** | "Your risk drops from 10% to 7%" (not "30% reduction") |
| **Use natural frequencies** | "3 out of 100 people" (rather than "3%") |
| **Use consistent denominators** | Compare "8 out of 100" vs. "5 out of 100" |
| **Visual aids improve understanding** | Icon arrays, pictographs, bar charts |
| **Avoid framing bias** | Present both positive (survival) and negative (mortality) frames |
| **Consider health literacy** | Use plain language; confirm with teach-back |

### 5.3.4 Practical Tools for Shared Decision-Making

| Tool | Description | Application |
|------|-------------|-------------|
| **Option Grid** | One-page summary comparing treatments on outcomes patients care about | Quick comparison of 2-3 options |
| **Decision Aid** | Evidence-based tool helping patients understand options and consider values | Formal pre-visit or in-visit tool |
| **Teach-Back Method** | Ask patient to explain back their understanding | Confirm comprehension |
| **BRAN Framework** | Benefits, Risks, Alternatives, Nothing — structured patient questioning | Empower patient inquiry |

### 5.3.5 The BRAN Framework for Patients

The BRAN framework helps patients structure their questions:

| Letter | Question | Purpose |
|--------|----------|---------|
| **B** | What are the **Benefits**? | Understand potential positive outcomes |
| **R** | What are the **Risks**? | Understand potential harms and side effects |
| **A** | What are the **Alternatives**? | Know all reasonable options |
| **N** | What happens if I do **Nothing**? | Understand natural history without intervention |

### 5.3.6 Evidence-Based SDM Example: Statin Therapy

**Clinical Scenario:** 60-year-old patient with 10-year ASCVD risk of 15%.

| Step | Dialogue Example |
|------|-----------------|
| **Explain risk** | "Your 10-year risk of heart attack or stroke is about 15%, or 15 out of 100 people like you" |
| **Present benefit** | "Taking a statin would reduce this to about 10% — that's 5 fewer heart attacks or strokes per 100 people" |
| **Translate to NNT** | "About 20 people like you need to take a statin for 5 years to prevent one heart attack or stroke" |
| **Present harms** | "About 5-10 out of 100 will develop muscle pain; about 1 in 200 will develop diabetes" |
| **Elicit values** | "What's most important to you? Preventing a heart attack? Avoiding medication? Avoiding muscle side effects?" |

## 5.4 Applying Guidelines to Individual Patients

### 5.4.1 Guideline Hierarchy in Primary Care

| Priority | Source Type | Examples |
|----------|------------|----------|
| **1 (Highest)** | International health organizations | WHO guidelines, CDC recommendations |
| **2** | National evidence-based guideline bodies | NICE (UK), USPSTF (US), NHMRC (Australia) |
| **3** | Specialty society guidelines | ACC/AHA, ESC, IDSA, AAFP, ACP |
| **4** | Consensus statements | Expert opinion where evidence is limited |
| **5** | Local institutional protocols | Hospital- or system-specific pathways |

### 5.4.2 Limitations of Guidelines

| Limitation | Description | Mitigation |
|-----------|-------------|-----------|
| **Population average** | Based on study populations that may differ from your patient | Consider patient characteristics relative to study populations |
| **Evidence gaps** | Many clinical questions lack high-quality evidence | Use lower-quality evidence with transparent acknowledgment |
| **Publication lag** | Guidelines may not reflect newest evidence | Monitor for guideline updates; consider recent RCTs |
| **Sponsorship bias** | Industry-funded guidelines may favor specific interventions | Check guideline funding sources; consult independent bodies |
| **One-size-fits-all** | May not account for comorbidities or patient preferences | Individualize using shared decision-making |
| **Regulatory variation** | Approved treatments vary by country | Follow local regulatory and formulary guidance |

### 5.4.3 Framework for Individualizing Guidelines

| Step | Action | Questions to Consider |
|------|--------|----------------------|
| **1. Identify applicable guideline** | Find most recent, relevant, high-quality guideline | Is this from a reputable source? When was it updated? |
| **2. Assess evidence quality** | Review GRADE ratings for specific recommendations | How strong is the evidence? How certain are the effects? |
| **3. Compare patient to study population** | Assess similarity to trial participants | Does my patient match the inclusion/exclusion criteria? |
| **4. Assess comorbidities** | Consider competing risks and life expectancy | Will this patient live long enough to benefit? |
| **5. Assess harms and burden** | Consider side effects, monitoring, cost | Are the harms acceptable to this patient? |
| **6. Elicit patient preferences** | Use shared decision-making | What does the patient value? |
| **7. Assess feasibility** | Consider access, cost, monitoring capacity | Can this be implemented practically? |
| **8. Decide and document** | Record reasoning | Why was this recommendation accepted, modified, or rejected? |

### 5.4.4 Special Considerations for Applying Evidence

| Population | Consideration |
|-----------|--------------|
| **Elderly patients** | Competing risks; life expectancy; polypharmacy; altered pharmacokinetics; frailty |
| **Patients with multimorbidity** | Guidelines often address single conditions; drug interactions; cumulative burden |
| **Pregnant patients** | Limited RCT data; fetal risk considerations; altered drug metabolism |
| **Pediatric patients** | Dosing differences; developmental considerations; limited trial data |
| **Patients with organ dysfunction** | Renal/hepatic dose adjustments; altered drug clearance |
| **Culturally diverse patients** | Health beliefs; communication barriers; differential treatment response |
| **Patients with limited health literacy** | Simplify regimens; use teach-back; visual aids |

### 5.4.5 Deprescribing and Rational Medication Use

| Principle | Application |
|-----------|------------|
| **Regular medication review** | At least annually; at care transitions; with new symptoms |
| **Start low, go slow** | Especially in elderly; half the usual starting dose |
| **One new drug at a time** | When possible, to identify adverse effects |
| **Consider deprescribing** | When risk exceeds benefit; when no longer indicated; when patient prefers |
| **Match treatment to life expectancy** | Avoid preventive medications when benefit timeline exceeds life expectancy |

**Common Deprescribing Candidates:**
- Proton pump inhibitors beyond 8 weeks without indication
- Benzodiazepines for chronic insomnia or anxiety (cognitive effects, fall risk)
- Anticholinergic medications (cognitive impairment, constipation, urinary retention)
- Dual antiplatelet therapy beyond guideline-recommended duration
- Diabetes medications with high hypoglycemia risk in elderly
- Cholinesterase inhibitors with minimal perceived benefit

# PART A: CARDIOVASCULAR MEDICINE

# Chapter 1: Hypertension

## 1.1 Overview

Hypertension (HTN) is defined as sustained elevation of systemic arterial blood pressure. It is the most common preventable risk factor for cardiovascular disease (CVD), ischemic stroke, hemorrhagic stroke, and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Approximately 46% of adults in the United States have hypertension, and only about 1 in 4 have their blood pressure under control. The 2017 ACC/AHA Guideline introduced a lower threshold for diagnosis compared to the earlier JNC-7 framework, effectively reclassifying millions of Americans as hypertensive and expanding the indication for treatment [^1^] [^23^].

**Pathophysiology (Brief):** Hypertension results from increased cardiac output, increased systemic vascular resistance, or both. Key mechanisms include: (1) dysregulation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), (2) sympathetic nervous system overactivity, (3) endothelial dysfunction with decreased nitric oxide bioavailability, (4) sodium retention and volume expansion, (5) vascular remodeling and stiffness, and (6) genetic and epigenetic factors. Over time, uncontrolled hypertension leads to target organ damage including left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), nephrosclerosis, retinopathy, and accelerated atherosclerosis.

**Epidemiology:** HTN affects approximately 1.28 billion adults worldwide. In the US, non-Hispanic Black adults have the highest prevalence (approximately 54%) and develop HTN earlier with greater severity than non-Hispanic White, Hispanic, and Asian adults. Only about 22% of adults with HTN have controlled BP (<130/80 mmHg).

## 1.2 Classification

### 1.2.1 Blood Pressure Categories (2017 ACC/AHA) [^1^] [^23^]

| Category | Systolic BP (mmHg) | | Diastolic BP (mmHg) |
|----------|-------------------|---|---------------------|
| Normal | <120 | and | <80 |
| Elevated | 120-129 | and | <80 |
| Stage 1 Hypertension | 130-139 | or | 80-89 |
| Stage 2 Hypertension | >=140 | or | >=90 |
| Hypertensive Crisis | >=180 | and/or | >=120 |

> **Key Points:** Adults with SBP and DBP in two different categories should be classified according to the higher category. Diagnosis requires an average of >=2 careful readings obtained on >=2 separate occasions. Out-of-office blood pressure monitoring (ambulatory blood pressure monitoring [ABPM] or home blood pressure monitoring [HBPM]) is recommended to confirm diagnosis and evaluate for white coat or masked hypertension.

### 1.2.2 Comparison: JNC-7 vs. 2017 ACC/AHA

| SBP (mmHg) | DBP (mmHg) | JNC-7 Classification | 2017 ACC/AHA Classification |
|------------|-----------|---------------------|----------------------------|
| <120 | <80 | Normal | Normal |
| 120-129 | <80 | Prehypertension | Elevated |
| 130-139 | 80-89 | Prehypertension | Stage 1 HTN |
| 140-159 | 90-99 | Stage 1 HTN | Stage 2 HTN |
| >=160 | >=100 | Stage 2 HTN | Stage 2 HTN |

> **Clinical Impact:** The 2017 ACC/AHA classification increases the prevalence of HTN from 32% (JNC-7) to 46% in US adults, but the number of adults requiring medication only increases modestly (from 31% to 36% of all US adults) because most newly classified patients fall into the Stage 1 category and have low cardiovascular risk, warranting lifestyle modification as first-line therapy.

## 1.3 Clinical Presentation

Hypertension is frequently asymptomatic, earning it the designation "silent killer." When symptoms do occur, they typically indicate target organ damage or a hypertensive emergency:

- **Headache:** Usually occipital, morning headaches; more common with severe hypertension (>=180/120 mmHg)
- **Dizziness:** Often medication-related or due to cerebrovascular involvement
- **Dyspnea:** Suggests left ventricular dysfunction or pulmonary edema
- **Chest pain:** May indicate concurrent CAD or aortic dissection (emergency)
- **Visual changes:** Blurred vision, scotomata (hypertensive retinopathy grade III-IV)
- **Epistaxis:** May occur with markedly elevated BP
- **Symptoms of secondary causes:** Muscle weakness (hypokalemia/aldosteronism), snoring/daytime somnolence (OSA), palpitations/tremor (pheochromocytoma), cold intolerance (hypothyroidism)

## 1.4 Diagnostic Workup

### 1.4.1 Proper Blood Pressure Measurement
- Patient seated quietly for 5 minutes, feet on floor, back supported
- Arm supported at heart level
- Appropriate cuff size (bladder encircling 80% of arm; use large adult cuff if arm circumference >32 cm, thigh cuff if >42 cm)
- No caffeine, exercise, or smoking for 30 minutes prior
- No talking during measurement
- Average of 2-3 readings, 1 minute apart
- Measure in both arms initially; use the higher reading arm for subsequent measurements
- If arm difference >10-15 mmHg, evaluate for subclavian stenosis or aortic coarctation

### 1.4.2 Initial Evaluation

| Component | Details |
|-----------|---------|
| **History** | Duration of HTN, prior readings, symptoms, family history, diet (sodium intake), physical activity, alcohol consumption, smoking, sleep history (snoring, witnessed apneas), medication adherence, all current medications (including OTC and supplements) |
| **Physical Exam** | Fundoscopic exam (arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, papilledema = grade IV), thyroid examination, cardiac auscultation (S4 gallop suggests LVH), abdominal bruits (renal artery stenosis), peripheral pulses (radio-femoral delay = coarctation), lower extremity edema |
| **Laboratory** | BMP (creatinine, eGFR, electrolytes), fasting glucose/HbA1c, lipid panel, TSH, urinalysis (protein; if positive, obtain albumin-to-creatinine ratio) |
| **Electrocardiogram** | Assess for LVH (Sokolow-Lyon criteria: S in V1 + R in V5 or V6 >35 mm), prior MI, arrhythmias |
| **Additional Testing** | Echocardiogram if concern for LV dysfunction, LVH, or valvular disease; ABPM for white coat/masked HTN evaluation; sleep study if OSA suspected; albumin-to-creatinine ratio if CKD or diabetes |

### 1.4.3 Secondary Hypertension Workup

> **Red Flag:** Secondary hypertension should be suspected when any of the following are present:
> - Onset <30 years without risk factors or obesity
> - Abrupt onset or worsening of previously controlled HTN
> - Resistant hypertension (>=3 drugs including a diuretic at maximally tolerated doses)
> - Target organ damage disproportionate to HTN duration
> - Hypokalemia with or without metabolic alkalosis (primary aldosteronism)
> - Abdominal bruit (renal artery stenosis)
> - Elevated creatinine after ACE-I/ARB initiation (bilateral renal artery stenosis)
> - Family history of kidney disease or early cerebrovascular accident
> - Episodic headache, sweating, and palpitations (pheochromocytoma)

**Common Secondary Causes:**

| Cause | Prevalence | Key Clues | Diagnostic Test |
|-------|-----------|-----------|-----------------|
| Primary aldosteronism | 5-10% of resistant HTN; ~2% of all HTN | Hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, muscle weakness | Aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) >20 ng/dL per ng/mL/hr (confirm with salt loading or fludrocortisone suppression test) |
| Renal artery stenosis | 1-5% | Abdominal bruit, flash pulmonary edema, unexplained kidney dysfunction, elevated creatinine with ACE-I/ARB | CTA/MRA renal arteries, duplex ultrasound (peak systolic velocity >180 cm/s or RAR >3.5) |
| Chronic kidney disease | Common (HTN both cause and consequence) | Elevated creatinine, proteinuria, anemia, metabolic acidosis | eGFR, urinalysis, renal ultrasound |
| Obstructive sleep apnea | Very common (50% of resistant HTN) | Snoring, daytime somnolence, obesity, resistant HTN | Polysomnography or home sleep apnea test |
| Pheochromocytoma | Rare (<0.2%) | Episodic headache, sweating, palpitations, tremor, anxiety, pallor | 24-hour urine or plasma metanephrines (sensitivity >95%) |
| Cushing syndrome | Rare | Central obesity, purple striae, proximal myopathy, easy bruising, hirsutism | 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (cortisol >1.8 mcg/dL = abnormal) |
| Coarctation of aorta | Rare (young patients) | Radio-femoral delay, arm-leg BP discrepancy >20 mmHg, systolic murmur posteriorly | CTA chest, echocardiography, MRA |
| Thyroid disease | Common (hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism) | Hyperthyroidism: tachycardia, tremor, weight loss, heat intolerance; Hypothyroidism: bradycardia, weight gain, cold intolerance, diastolic HTN | TSH, free T4 |
| Drug-induced | Common | Review all medications and supplements | Medication history |

**Common Culprit Drugs:** NSAIDs (inhibit prostaglandins), oral contraceptives (estrogen activates RAAS), systemic corticosteroids (mineralocorticoid effect), decongestants (pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine are sympathomimetics), stimulants (amphetamines, cocaine), erythropoietin (increases blood viscosity and vascular resistance), calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus cause vasoconstriction and sodium retention), licorice (mineralocorticoid effect), herbal supplements (ephedra, yohimbine).

## 1.5 Management

### 1.5.1 Lifestyle Modifications (All Patients) [^1^]

| Modification | Recommendation | Expected BP Reduction |
|-------------|----------------|---------------------|
| **Weight loss** | Achieve/maintain ideal body weight (BMI 18.5-24.9); aim for 1-2 lb/week loss through caloric deficit | 5-20 mmHg per 10 kg lost |
| **DASH diet** | Emphasize fruits (4-5 servings/day), vegetables (4-5 servings/day), whole grains, low-fat dairy (2-3 servings/day); reduce saturated fat (<6% of calories) and cholesterol (<150 mg/day) | 8-14 mmHg |
| **Sodium restriction** | <2,300 mg/day (ideally <1,500 mg/day); gradual reduction to improve adherence | 2-8 mmHg |
| **Physical activity** | >=150 min/week moderate-intensity aerobic activity (e.g., brisk walking, cycling, swimming) or 75 min/week vigorous; add resistance training 2x/week | 4-9 mmHg |
| **Alcohol moderation** | Men: <=2 standard drinks/day; Women: <=1 drink/day; 1 standard drink = 14 g alcohol | 2-4 mmHg |
| **Smoking cessation** | Absolute requirement; combine behavioral counseling with pharmacotherapy (varenicline, bupropion, NRT); provides immediate CVD risk reduction | Immediate CVD risk reduction |
| **Potassium intake** | 3,500-5,000 mg/day through diet (fruits, vegetables, legumes) if no CKD Stage 3b-5 or hyperkalemia risk | 4-5 mmHg |
| **Stress reduction** | Meditation, yoga, biofeedback, cognitive behavioral therapy, adequate sleep (7-9 hours) | Variable (2-5 mmHg) |

> **Note:** Combined lifestyle modifications can achieve BP reductions comparable to single-drug therapy (10-20 mmHg), making them essential for all patients regardless of pharmacologic treatment needs.

### 1.5.2 Pharmacologic Treatment [^1^] [^23^]

**Treatment Thresholds:**
- **Stage 1 HTN (130-139/80-89):** Initiate pharmacologic therapy if clinical CVD or 10-year ASCVD risk >=10%. If ASCVD risk <10%, start with lifestyle modification for 3-6 months, then reassess.
- **Stage 2 HTN (>=140/90):** Initiate pharmacologic therapy plus lifestyle modification (two first-line agents of different classes preferred for Stage 2).
- **Target BP:** <130/80 mmHg for most adults (if tolerated). For adults >=65 years in the community, SBP target <130 mmHg is reasonable if tolerated.

**First-Line Antihypertensive Agents:**

| Class | Examples | Starting Dose | Target Dose | Key Considerations | Contraindications |
|-------|----------|--------------|-------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| **Thiazide diuretics** | Chlorthalidone 12.5-25 mg daily; HCTZ 12.5-25 mg daily; Indapamide 1.25 mg daily | 12.5 mg | 25-50 mg | Chlorthalidone preferred (longer half-life, better outcomes in ALLHAT); monitor K+, creatinine, glucose, uric acid | Severe electrolyte disturbances, severe hyponatremia |
| **ACE inhibitors** | Lisinopril 5-10 mg daily; Enalapril 5 mg BID | 5 mg | 10-40 mg | First-line with CKD, diabetes; check creatinine and K+ at 1-2 weeks; cough in 5-10%; angioedema in 0.1-0.7% | Pregnancy, bilateral RAS, history of angioedema |
| **ARBs** | Losartan 25-50 mg daily; Valsartan 40-80 mg daily; Olmesartan 20 mg daily | 25 mg | 50-150 mg | Alternative to ACE-I if cough; similar renal protective effects; direct vasodilation of efferent arteriole | Pregnancy, bilateral RAS |
| **Dihydropyridine CCBs** | Amlodipine 2.5-5 mg daily; Nifedipine ER 30 mg daily | 2.5 mg | 5-10 mg | Effective in Black patients; peripheral edema common (dose-dependent); no metabolic adverse effects | HFrEF (relative; may worsen edema) |
| **Non-DHP CCBs** | Diltiazem ER 120-240 mg daily; Verapamil ER 120-240 mg daily | 120 mg | 240-480 mg | Useful with atrial arrhythmias (rate control); negative inotrope and chronotrope | HFrEF, severe bradycardia (<50 bpm), 2nd/3rd degree AV block |

**Compelling Indications (Guideline-Directed Specific Agents):**

| Condition | Recommended Agents | Evidence |
|-----------|-------------------|----------|
| HFrEF | ACE-I/ARB/ARNI + beta-blocker + MRA + SGLT2i | Class I, Level A (2022 ACC/AHA/HFSA) |
| Post-MI | ACE-I + beta-blocker + MRA + high-intensity statin | Class I, Level A |
| CKD with albuminuria | ACE-I or ARB (maximally tolerated dose) | Class I, Level A |
| Diabetes | ACE-I or ARB preferred; add CCB or thiazide as needed | Class I, Level A |
| Coronary artery disease | Beta-blocker + ACE-I + high-intensity statin | Class I, Level A |
| Recurrent stroke prevention | Thiazide + ACE-I (PROGRESS trial) | Class I, Level A |
| Black patients (without CKD/CVD) | Thiazide diuretic or CCB preferred as initial agent | ALLHAT trial demonstrated superiority |

**Combination Therapy:**
- Most patients will require >=2 agents to reach BP target (approximately 75% of hypertensive adults need multiple drugs).
- **Preferred combinations:** ACE-I/ARB + CCB or ACE-I/ARB + thiazide diuretic.
- Single-pill combinations improve adherence by 20-30%.
- **Avoid:** ACE-I + ARB combination (increased adverse events including hyperkalemia and AKI; no outcome benefit per ALTITUDE and VA NEPHRON-D trials).
- If three drugs needed: ACE-I/ARB + CCB + thiazide is preferred triple combination.
- Consider loop diuretics (furosemide) instead of thiazides if eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73m2 (thiazides are ineffective at low GFR).

### 1.5.3 Resistant Hypertension

**Definition:** Blood pressure remains >=130/80 mmHg despite concurrent use of 3 antihypertensive agents of different classes at maximally tolerated doses, one of which is a diuretic. OR controlled BP requiring >=4 agents.

**Systematic Approach:**

1. **Confirm adherence:** Non-adherence is the most common cause of apparent resistant HTN (affects 30-50% of apparent resistant cases). Use pharmacy refill data, direct questioning, and urine/plasma drug levels if available.
2. **Confirm proper BP measurement technique:** Use correct cuff size, position, adequate rest period; consider out-of-office BP monitoring to exclude white coat effect.
3. **Screen for secondary causes:** Primary aldosteronism is the most common (screen with ARR), followed by renal artery stenosis and OSA.
4. **Optimize current regimen:** Ensure diuretic is at adequate dose; switch from HCTZ to chlorthalidone (12.5-25 mg) or indapamide (1.25 mg) if needed; consider using a loop diuretic if eGFR <45.
5. **Add spironolactone:** PATHWAY-2 trial demonstrated spironolactone (25-50 mg daily) is the most effective 4th-line agent (superior to bisoprolol and doxazosin). Monitor K+ and creatinine at 1 week, 1 month, then quarterly.
6. **Other 4th-line options:** Beta-blockers (if not already used), alpha-blockers (doxazosin 1-8 mg daily), central alpha-2 agonists (clonidine 0.1-0.3 mg BID or patch), or direct vasodilators (hydralazine 25-100 mg TID-QID, minoxidil 2.5-40 mg daily - last resort due to hirsutism and fluid retention).
7. **Referral:** To hypertension specialist or nephrologist for confirmed resistant HTN.
8. **Renal denervation:** Consider for select patients with confirmed resistant HTN despite optimal medical therapy (SYMPLICITY HTN-3 and subsequent trials show modest benefit of approximately 5-10 mmHg reduction).

## 1.6 Special Populations

| Population | Considerations | Preferred Agents | Target BP |
|------------|---------------|------------------|-----------|
| **Pregnancy** | Hypertensive disorders complicate 5-10% of pregnancies; monitor for preeclampsia (new-onset HTN + proteinuria + end-organ dysfunction after 20 weeks) | Labetalol, nifedipine ER, methyldopa (safest evidence base) | <140/90 mmHg (acute); <140/90 mmHg (chronic) |
| | **Contraindicated:** ACE-I, ARB, DRI (direct renin inhibitor) - teratogenic (renal agenesis, oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia) | | |
| **Children/Adolescents** | BP >=95th percentile for age/sex/height; use pediatric cuffs; evaluate for secondary causes (coarctation, renal disease, endocrine) | ACE-I, ARB, CCB, thiazide | <90th percentile for age/sex/height |
| **Elderly (>65)** | Target <130 mmHg SBP if tolerated; increased risk of orthostatic hypotension; "start low, go slow" principle; monitor for falls | Any first-line; avoid orthostatic hypotension; consider deprescribing if symptomatic | <130/80 (if tolerated); avoid SBP <120 |
| **Black adults** | Higher prevalence (54%), earlier onset, greater severity, higher risk of CKD and stroke; thiazide or CCB preferred initial agents; ACE-I/ARB less effective as monotherapy due to lower renin levels | Thiazide, CCB; combination therapy often needed | <130/80 |
| **CKD (eGFR <60)** | ACE-I or ARB if albuminuria (reduces progression); loop diuretics preferred if eGFR <30 (thiazides ineffective); watch for hyperkalemia | ACE-I/ARB (albuminuria), loop diuretics | <130/80 |
| **Diabetes** | ACE-I or ARB preferred (renoprotective); intensive BP control reduces microvascular complications; SGLT2i and GLP-1 RA provide additional CV benefit | ACE-I/ARB + CCB or thiazide | <130/80 |
| **Post-stroke** | Gradual BP reduction over days to weeks; avoid precipitous drops (cerebral autoregulation is impaired); benefit established for secondary prevention | Thiazide + ACE-I (PROGRESS trial) | <130/80 |
| **Coronary artery disease** | Beta-blocker + ACE-I/ARB; avoid excessive DBP lowering (<60 mmHg may compromise coronary perfusion) | Beta-blocker + ACE-I + CCB or thiazide | <130/80 |

## 1.7 Red Flags / Emergency Features

> **CRITICAL: Hypertensive Emergency vs. Urgency**
>
> **Hypertensive Emergency** (BP >=180/120 mmHg WITH acute target organ damage): This is a medical emergency requiring immediate IV therapy and intensive care admission. Acute target organ damage includes:
> - Hypertensive encephalopathy (altered mental status, headache, seizures, visual changes, papilledema)
> - Acute stroke (ischemic or hemorrhagic)
> - Acute coronary syndrome
> - Acute aortic dissection
> - Acute pulmonary edema
> - Acute kidney injury (acute tubular necrosis from malignant HTN)
> - Eclampsia/preeclampsia with severe features
> - Pheochromocytoma crisis
> - Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes on peripheral smear)
>
> **Hypertensive Urgency** (BP >=180/120 mmHg WITHOUT target organ damage): Not a true emergency. Do NOT acutely lower BP in the ED or outpatient setting. Gradual reduction over 24-48 hours with oral agents. Rapid reduction risks cerebral, coronary, and renal hypoperfusion.

**Hypertensive Emergency Treatment Principles:**
- Reduce mean arterial pressure (MAP) by no more than 10-20% in the first hour
- Reduce to approximately 160/100-110 mmHg over the next 2-6 hours
- Normal BP should be achieved over days, not hours
- Avoid precipitous drops (risk of cerebral, coronary, and renal hypoperfusion)

| Agent | Dosing | Indications | Cautions |
|-------|--------|-------------|----------|
| **Nicardipine** | 5 mg/hr IV infusion, titrate by 2.5 mg/hr q5min; max 15 mg/hr | Most hypertensive emergencies (except acute HF) | Tachycardia, headache, flushing; requires arterial line for titration |
| **Clevidipine** | 1-2 mg/hr IV, double q90sec until effect; max 32 mg/hr | Perioperative HTN, aortic dissection, when rapid titration needed | Contraindicated with soy/egg allergy, lipid disorders; requires line changes q12h |
| **Nitroprusside** | 0.3-10 mcg/kg/min IV (start 0.25-0.5 mcg/kg/min) | Aortic dissection, acute pulmonary edema, perioperative HTN | Cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity with prolonged use (>48-72h) or high doses; light-sensitive |
| **Labetalol** | 20 mg IV over 2 min, then 20-80 mg q10min OR 1-2 mg/min infusion | Most emergencies; preferred in pregnancy; perioperative | Bronchospasm (non-selective beta-blockade), bradycardia, heart block; avoid in acute decompensated HF |
| **Esmolol** | 500 mcg/kg IV bolus, then 50-200 mcg/kg/min infusion | Aortic dissection, perioperative HTN; when ultra-short acting needed | Very short half-life (9 min); bradycardia; avoid in HF |
| **Hydralazine** | 10-20 mg IV q4-6h (IM not recommended - unpredictable absorption) | Eclampsia/preeclampsia (with magnesium sulfate) | Reflex tachycardia; unpredictable BP response; less preferred |
| **Fenoldopam** | 0.1-0.3 mcg/kg/min IV | HTN emergency with renal impairment (dopamine-1 agonist - preserves renal blood flow) | Tachycardia, headache, glaucoma (increases intraocular pressure) |

**Condition-Specific IV Agents:**
- **Aortic dissection:** Beta-blockade first (labetalol or esmolol) + vasodilator (nitroprusside or nicardipine) - NEVER use vasodilator alone (increases shear stress on aorta)
- **Acute pulmonary edema:** Nitroglycerin (vasodilation + preload reduction) + loop diuretics; avoid hydralazine
- **Acute ischemic stroke:** Permissive hypertension (SBP up to 220 mmHg for first 48-72 hours unless IV thrombolysis or endovascular therapy planned); if thrombolysis candidate, lower to <185 mmHg systolic
- **Intracerebral hemorrhage:** SBP target 140-160 mmHg (systolic reduction to 140 mmHg is safe and may improve functional outcomes per ATACH-2 trial)
- **Preeclampsia/eclampsia:** Labetalol, hydralazine, or nifedipine; magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis; definitive treatment is delivery

## 1.8 Follow-up and Monitoring

| BP Severity | Initial Follow-up | Evaluation |
|-------------|-------------------|------------|
| Elevated (120-129/<80) | 3-6 months | Lifestyle counseling; reassess need for pharmacotherapy based on ASCVD risk |
| Stage 1 HTN (130-139/80-89) | 1 month after initiating therapy; then every 3-6 months | Check adherence, side effects, home BP readings |
| Stage 2 HTN (>=140/90) | 2-4 weeks after initiating therapy; then every 1-3 months | More frequent monitoring until controlled |
| Resistant HTN | Every 2-4 weeks until controlled; then every 1-3 months | Laboratory monitoring, side effect assessment |

**Laboratory Monitoring:**
- BMP (K+, creatinine) 1-2 weeks after starting ACE-I/ARB or diuretic, then every 3-6 months
- Annual lipid panel, HbA1c, urinalysis
- Consider ABPM if office-home BP discrepancy suspected
- Review medication adherence at every visit

## 1.9 When to Seek Emergency Care

Seek emergency medical attention immediately if:
- Blood pressure >=180/120 mmHg accompanied by symptoms (headache, chest pain, shortness of breath, visual changes, confusion, seizures, severe back pain)
- Blood pressure >=220/140 mmHg regardless of symptoms
- Symptoms of stroke (sudden weakness, difficulty speaking, facial droop)
- Symptoms of heart attack (chest pressure, radiation to arm/jaw, diaphoresis, nausea)
- Pregnancy with blood pressure >=160/110 or symptoms of preeclampsia (severe headache, visual changes, right upper quadrant pain, swelling)
