# Chapter 10: Male Infertility

---

## 10.1 Clinical Overview

Infertility affects approximately 15% of couples globally. Male factor infertility contributes to approximately 40-50% of infertility cases, either as sole cause or combined with female factors. Male infertility is defined as the inability of a couple to achieve pregnancy after 12 months of unprotected intercourse (or 6 months if female partner >35 years old).

## 10.2 Evaluation

### 10.2.1 Initial Assessment

**Comprehensive History:**

| Category | Key Questions |
|----------|--------------|
| **Medical** | Chronic illnesses (diabetes, thyroid, celiac, CRF, liver disease), infections (mumps orchitis, STIs), genetic conditions |
| **Surgical** | Hernia repair, orchiopexy, varicocelectomy, vasectomy, pelvic/abdominal surgery, prostate surgery |
| **Developmental** | Cryptorchidism history, delayed puberty, testicular trauma/torsion |
| **Sexual** | Erectile function, ejaculatory function, timing/frequency of intercourse, use of lubricants (many are spermicidal) |
| **Family** | Infertility, genetic conditions, birth defects |
| **Environmental/Occupational** | Heat exposure (saunas, hot tubs, occupational), pesticides, solvents, heavy metals, radiation |
| **Medications/Substances** | Testosterone, anabolic steroids, finasteride, SSRIs, alcohol, tobacco, marijuana, opioids |

**Physical Examination:**
- Testicular volume: Use Prader orchidometer (normal adult >=15 mL, or length >=4 cm)
- Testicular consistency: Normal testes are firm and resilient; soft testes suggest impaired spermatogenesis
- Varicocele: Palpate in standing and supine positions, with and without Valsalva
- Secondary sexual characteristics: Body hair distribution, gynecomastia, facial hair
- Penile examination: Peyronie plaques, hypospadias, phimosis
- Digital rectal exam if indicated
- Assess for signs of hypogonadism

### 10.2.2 Semen Analysis (WHO 6th Edition, 2021) [^421^]

**Collection requirements:**
- 2-7 days of sexual abstinence before collection
- Two separate samples collected 2-3 weeks apart (high variability between samples)
- Complete collection in clean container; note any spillage
- Deliver to lab within 30-60 minutes; keep at body temperature during transport

**WHO 2021 Lower Reference Limits (5th percentile):**

| Parameter | Lower Reference Limit |
|-----------|----------------------|
| **Semen volume** | >=1.4 mL |
| **Sperm concentration** | >=16 million/mL |
| **Total sperm count** | >=39 million per ejaculate |
| **Total motility** (progressive + non-progressive) | >=42% |
| **Progressive motility** | >=30% |
| **Normal morphology** (strict/Kruger criteria) | >=4% |
| **Vitality** (live sperm) | >=54% |
| **pH** | >=7.2 |

**Additional tests (when indicated):**
- **Post-ejaculate urinalysis:** To diagnose retrograde ejaculation (sperm present in urine)
- **Antisperm antibodies:** Post-vasectomy, trauma, infection, varicocele; sperm agglutination on analysis
- **Semen culture:** If infection suspected
- **Fructose:** Absent fructose suggests ejaculatory duct obstruction or seminal vesicle agenesis

### 10.2.3 Hormonal Testing

| Hormone | Interpretation | Clinical Significance |
|---------|---------------|---------------------|
| **FSH** | Elevated | Primary testicular failure (Sertoli cell damage) |
| **FSH** | Low/normal | Secondary (hypogonadotropic) hypogonadism |
| **LH + Testosterone** | Both low | Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (hypothalamic/pituitary) |
| **LH high + Testosterone low** | Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (primary testicular failure) |
| **Prolactin** | Elevated | Prolactinoma; suppresses GnRH; check if secondary hypogonadism |
| **Estradiol** | Elevated | Obesity (peripheral aromatization); may suppress HPG axis |

**Indications for hormonal testing:**
- Abnormal semen analysis (especially severe oligospermia or azoospermia)
- Signs of hypogonadism
- Suspected endocrine disorder
- Prior to initiating hormonal therapy for fertility

### 10.2.4 Genetic Testing

| Test | Indication | What It Detects |
|------|-----------|----------------|
| **Karyotype** | Severe oligospermia (<5 million/mL) or non-obstructive azoospermia | Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY); sex chromosome abnormalities |
| **Y-chromosome microdeletion** | Severe oligospermia or NOA | Microdeletions in AZF (azoospermia factor) regions a-d; guides TESE prognosis |
| **CFTR mutation testing** | Azoospermia with absent vas deferens (CBAVD) | Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator mutations |
| **Karyotype + microarray** | Recurrent pregnancy loss | Balanced translocations |

### 10.2.5 Additional Testing

| Test | Indication |
|------|-----------|
| **Scrotal ultrasound** | Varicocele, testicular masses, microlithiasis, small testes, absence of vas deferens |
| **Transrectal ultrasound (TRUS)** | Ejaculatory duct obstruction (dilated seminal vesicles), prostate pathology |
| **Testicular biopsy** | Part of TESE procedure for NOA; diagnostic if endocrine workup unrevealing |
| **MRI sella** | Elevated prolactin or other pituitary signs |

## 10.3 Causes and Treatment

### Classification by Anatomic/Physiologic Level

| Category | Causes | Treatment |
|----------|--------|-----------|
| **Pretesticular (endocrine/hypothalamic-pituitary)** | Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, hyperprolactinemia, thyroid disease, hemochromatosis, Cushing syndrome, exogenous steroids | Hormonal therapy (hCG + FSH or pulsatile GnRH); treat underlying endocrinopathy |
| **Testicular** | Varicocele, cryptorchidism, orchitis, testicular cancer, genetic (Klinefelter, Y-microdeletion), chemotherapy/radiation, anabolic steroid use | Varicocelectomy; sperm retrieval + ART; avoid gonadotoxins |
| **Post-testicular (obstructive)** | Vasectomy, CBAVD, ejaculatory duct obstruction, epididymal obstruction (infection/inflammation) | Vasectomy reversal; transurethral resection of ejaculatory ducts; epididymovasostomy; sperm retrieval + ICSI |
| **Sexual dysfunction** | ED, retrograde ejaculation, anejaculation, premature ejaculation | Treat underlying sexual dysfunction; IUI if retrograde ejaculation |
| **Idiopathic** | No identifiable cause (~25-30%) | Empiric treatment or ART |

### 10.3.1 Specific Treatment Approaches

**Varicocele Treatment:**
- Indication: Palpable varicocele + abnormal semen analysis + infertility OR testicular growth arrest in adolescent
- Microsurgical varicocelectomy: Gold standard; semen parameters improve in 60-80%; natural pregnancy rates 30-50%
- Consider repair even if only mildly abnormal SA if female partner has normal fertility

**Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism:**
- hCG 1,000-2,000 IU 2-3x/week (stimulates Leydig cells)
- Add FSH or recombinant FSH 75-150 IU 3x/week if spermatogenesis not achieved in 6 months (stimulates Sertoli cells)
- Response may take 6-12 months or longer
- If treatment started before puberty, higher doses and longer time needed

**Ejaculatory Duct Obstruction:**
- TRUS-guided transurethral resection of ejaculatory ducts (TURED)
- Postoperative semen analysis to confirm patency

**Azoospermia Workup and Treatment:**

| Type | Diagnosis | Treatment |
|------|-----------|-----------|
| **Obstructive azoospermia (OA)** | Normal FSH, normal testicular volume, normal testosterone; dilated epididymis or absent vas; previous vasectomy | Vasectomy reversal; epididymovasostomy; MESA/TESE + ICSI |
| **Non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA)** | Elevated FSH, small testes, low/normal testosterone; testicular failure | Micro-TESE (microsurgical testicular sperm extraction); sperm found in 40-60% of cases; ICSI required |

### 10.3.2 Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART)

| Procedure | Indication | Description |
|-----------|-----------|-------------|
| **Intrauterine insemination (IUI)** | Mild male factor (mild oligospermia, motility issues); cervical factor; unexplained infertility | Washed, concentrated sperm placed directly into uterus at time of ovulation |
| **In-vitro fertilization (IVF)** | Moderate male factor; tubal factor; endometriosis; unexplained infertility | Ovarian stimulation, egg retrieval, fertilization in laboratory, embryo transfer |
| **Intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI)** | Severe male factor (severe oligospermia, teratozoospermia); prior fertilization failure; sperm retrieved surgically | Single sperm injected directly into oocyte cytoplasm; enables fertilization with very low sperm counts |
| **Testicular sperm extraction (TESE)** | Azoospermia | Open surgical sperm retrieval from testis |
| **Micro-TESE** | Non-obstructive azoospermia | Microsurgical dissection under operating microscope to identify sperm-producing tubules |
| **Microsurgical epididymal sperm aspiration (MESA)** | Obstructive azoospermia | Sperm aspirated from epididymis under microsurgical visualization |
| **Percutaneous epididymal sperm aspiration (PESA)** | Obstructive azoospermia | Needle aspiration of epididymis (less invasive than MESA) |

### 10.3.3 Empiric Medical Therapies

| Therapy | Evidence | Notes |
|---------|----------|-------|
| **Clomiphene citrate** | Moderate | For men with low-normal testosterone and idiopathic oligospermia; off-label |
| **Antioxidants** (CoQ10, vitamin E, zinc, folic acid, L-carnitine, selenium) | Limited/uncertain | May improve sperm parameters in some men; generally safe |
| **Human growth hormone** | Limited | Not routinely recommended |
| **Anti-estrogens** (tamoxifen) | Limited | May improve sperm count in some men with elevated estradiol |

## 10.4 Counseling and Prevention

### General Recommendations to Optimize Fertility

| Recommendation | Rationale |
|---------------|-----------|
| Maintain healthy weight (BMI 18.5-25) | Obesity impairs sperm quality via hormonal and thermal mechanisms |
| Avoid tobacco | Reduces sperm count, motility, and morphology |
| Limit alcohol | Heavy use reduces testosterone and sperm quality |
| Avoid recreational drugs (marijuana, cocaine, anabolic steroids) | All impair spermatogenesis; anabolic steroids cause profound suppression |
| Avoid excessive heat (saunas, hot tubs, tight underwear) | Elevated scrotal temperature impairs sperm production |
| Manage medical conditions (diabetes, thyroid, varicocele) | Underlying conditions can impair fertility |
| Review medications with physician | Some medications impair fertility (testosterone, finasteride, SSRIs, calcium channel blockers) |
| Consider antioxidant supplementation | May provide modest benefit; generally safe |
| Regular exercise | Improves overall health and may improve sperm quality |

### When to Refer

- Azoospermia or severe oligospermia (<5 million/mL)
- Abnormal hormonal profile
- Suspected obstructive cause
- Need for surgical intervention (varicocelectomy, vasectomy reversal)
- Need for assisted reproductive technology
- Complex genetic findings
- Couple infertility >1 year with identified male factor

# Emergency Reference: Red Flags

---

## Women's Health Emergencies

| Condition | Red Flags | Immediate Action |
|-----------|-----------|-----------------|
| **Ectopic pregnancy** | Amenorrhea + abdominal pain + vaginal bleeding + hemodynamic instability; shoulder pain (referred); syncope | IV access, type & screen, quantitative hCG, stat pelvic ultrasound; surgical/emergency OB consult |
| **Ovarian torsion** | Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain with nausea/vomiting; adnexal mass | Emergent surgical consult; ultrasound with Doppler; do not delay surgical exploration |
| **Ruptured hemorrhagic cyst/ectopic** | Acute pelvic pain with hemodynamic instability; syncope; acute abdomen | Fluid resuscitation; emergent surgical management |
| **Septic abortion/PID with sepsis** | Fever >38.5 C, severe pelvic pain, purulent discharge, tachycardia, hypotension | Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics; hospital admission; source control |
| **Eclampsia** | Seizure in pregnant/postpartum woman with preeclampsia | Airway protection; magnesium sulfate 4-6 g IV load; BP control; emergent delivery |
| **HELLP syndrome** | RUQ/epigastric pain, thrombocytopenia, elevated LFTs in pregnancy | Hospital admission; magnesium sulfate; BP control; emergent delivery if >=34 weeks or deteriorating |
| **Postpartum hemorrhage** | Blood loss >500 mL (vaginal) or >1000 mL (cesarean); signs of shock | Uterine massage; uterotonics (oxytocin, methylergonovine, carboprost, misoprostol); surgical intervention |
| **Postpartum psychosis** | Delusions, hallucinations, extreme confusion, homicidal/suicidal ideation within first 2 weeks postpartum | Emergency psychiatric hospitalization; medical emergency |

## Men's Health Emergencies

| Condition | Red Flags | Immediate Action |
|-----------|-----------|-----------------|
| **Testicular torsion** | Acute severe scrotal pain, absent cremasteric reflex, elevated/h horizontally lying testis, nausea/vomiting | Emergent urology consult; surgical exploration within 6 hours for best salvage |
| **Acute urinary retention** | Painful bladder distension, inability to void, suprapubic tenderness | Bladder catheterization (urethral or suprapubic); evaluate cause; alpha-blocker if BPH |
| **Fournier gangrene** | Perineal/genital pain, swelling, crepitus, fever, necrosis, sepsis; disproportionate pain | Emergency surgical debridement; broad-spectrum IV antibiotics; ICU admission; high mortality |
| **Priapism** | Painful erection >4 hours duration; ischemic (low-flow) vs. non-ischemic (high-flow) | Ischemic priapism: Emergency - corpus cavernosum aspiration + irrigation with phenylephrine; urology consult |
| **Acute bacterial prostatitis with sepsis** | Fever, rigors, dysuria, perineal pain, hypotension, confusion | IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone + fluoroquinolone); hospital admission; suprapubic catheter if retention |
| **Paraphimosis** | Retracted foreskin proximal to glans causing painful glans swelling, edema, discoloration | Manual reduction (compress glans to reduce edema, then advance foreskin); dorsal slit or circumcision if unable |
| **Penile fracture** | Sudden cracking/popping sound during intercourse, immediate detumescence, swelling, ecchymosis ("eggplant deformity"), pain | Surgical repair within 24 hours; urology emergency |

| Gail Model | https://bcrisktool.cancer.gov/ | Breast cancer risk for chemoprevention eligibility |
| IPSS Calculator | Various medical apps | BPH symptom severity |
| SHIM (IIEF-5) | Various medical apps | ED severity assessment |
| PSA Decision Framework | AUA Guidelines | Prostate cancer screening decisions |
| NCCN Guidelines | https://www.nccn.org/guidelines/ | Cancer screening and management |

# Chapter 1: Vaccination Guidelines

## 1.1 Overview

Vaccination remains one of the most effective preventive interventions in modern medicine. The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) publishes annual immunization schedules incorporating new evidence throughout the year. This chapter provides comprehensive guidance on adult vaccination based on the 2024-2025 ACIP schedule, including key updates and special populations. [^274^] [^276^]

**Key 2025 Schedule Changes:**
- Transition from quadrivalent to **trivalent influenza vaccines** (IIV3, aIIV3, HD-IIV3, RIV3) [^456^]
- Updated **COVID-19 vaccine** recommendations with 2024-2025 formulation
- Addition of **21-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV21; CAPVAXIVE)** as an option [^467^]
- Addition of **inactivated polio vaccine (IPV)** to adult tables [^456^]
- Updated **respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)** recommendations [^452^]
- New **mRNA RSV vaccine (mResvia)** added [^456^]

**How to Use the Schedule:**
1. Determine recommended vaccines by age (Table 1)
2. Assess need for additional vaccines by medical condition/indication (Table 2)
3. Review vaccine types, dosing, intervals, and special situations
4. Review contraindications and precautions
5. Review new/updated ACIP guidance (Addendum) [^276^]

---

## 1.2 Influenza Vaccine

### Overview
Annual influenza vaccination is recommended for all adults 19 years and older. Influenza causes significant morbidity and mortality, particularly in older adults, immunocompromised persons, and those with chronic medical conditions.

### Recommendations

| Population | Recommendation | Evidence Level |
|------------|---------------|----------------|
| All adults 19+ | Annual vaccination | ACIP universal recommendation [^276^] |
| Adults 65+ | HD-IIV3, aIIV3, or RIV3 **preferred** over standard-dose | ACIP preferential recommendation [^276^] |
| Egg allergy | Any age-appropriate influenza vaccine (egg-based or non-egg-based) acceptable | ACIP [^274^] |
| Pregnant women | Inactivated influenza vaccine (not LAIV) | ACIP; safe in any trimester |
| Solid organ transplant (19-64) | HD-IIV3 and aIIV3 acceptable options | ACIP [^274^] |

### Key Clinical Points
- **Trivalent formulation** replaces quadrivalent for the 2024-25 season (B/Yamagata lineage removed due to absence of circulating virus) [^456^]
- Vaccination ideally completed by end of October, but continue vaccinating as long as influenza is circulating
- It takes approximately 2 weeks after vaccination for antibodies to develop
- **LAIV3 contraindication:** Close contacts of severely immunosuppressed persons requiring protected environment should NOT receive live attenuated influenza vaccine [^274^]
- Common adverse effects: soreness at injection site, low-grade fever, mild myalgias (1-2 days)

---

## 1.3 COVID-19 Vaccine

### Overview
COVID-19 vaccination remains an essential preventive measure. Updated formulations are released annually to address circulating variants. [^274^] [^276^]

### 2024-2025 Recommendations by Population

| Population | Vaccination Schedule |
|------------|---------------------|
| Adults 19-64 (unvaccinated) | 1 dose updated 2024-25 Moderna or Pfizer-BioNTech; OR 2 doses Novavax at 0, 3-8 weeks |
| Adults 19-64 (previously vaccinated) | 1 dose updated 2024-25 vaccine at least 8 weeks after most recent dose |
| Adults 65+ | 2 doses updated 2024-25 vaccine, minimum 2 months apart [^276^] |
| Immunocompromised adults | May receive additional doses beyond routine; 3-dose initial mRNA series, followed by boosters |
| Pregnancy | Recommended during pregnancy; safe at any gestational age [^542^] |

### Key Clinical Points
- Use vaccine from same manufacturer for all doses in initial series when possible
- Common adverse effects: injection site pain, fatigue, headache, myalgia, fever (typically resolve within 1-3 days)
- Rare: myocarditis/pericarditis (higher risk in young males after mRNA vaccines; typically mild and self-limited)
- Contraindications: Severe allergic reaction (e.g., anaphylaxis) to previous dose or component

---

## 1.4 Tdap/Td (Tetanus, Diphtheria, Pertussis)

### Overview
Tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis are vaccine-preventable diseases with significant morbidity and mortality. Pertussis (whooping cough) has resurged in adults due to waning immunity, making Tdap vaccination particularly important for preventing infant transmission. [^534^] [^535^]

### Recommendations

| Scenario | Recommendation |
|----------|---------------|
| Primary series (unvaccinated adults) | 3 doses Td-containing vaccine: Tdap, then Td/Tdap at 4 weeks, then Td/Tdap at 6-12 months [^534^] |
| Booster (all adults) | Td or Tdap every 10 years throughout life |
| Adults never received Tdap | Single dose of Tdap regardless of interval since last Td [^274^] |
| Pregnancy | Tdap during **each pregnancy**, 27-36 weeks gestation; if not given during pregnancy, give immediately postpartum [^538^] [^543^] |
| Wound management | Tdap if >5 years since last booster, regardless of gestational age [^546^] |

### Pregnancy Considerations
- Tdap at 27-36 weeks gestation reduces infant pertussis risk by **78%** in babies <2 months old [^543^]
- Earlier vaccination within the 27-36 week window maximizes passive antibody transfer to the newborn
- If tetanus booster is indicated during pregnancy (>10 years since prior Td), give Tdap at 27-36 weeks rather than Td

---

## 1.5 HPV Vaccine (Gardasil 9)

### Overview
Human papillomavirus (HPV) is the most common sexually transmitted infection and causes cervical, anal, oropharyngeal, vulvar, vaginal, and penile cancers. HPV vaccination prevents new infections but does NOT treat existing infections. [^464^]

### Recommendations

| Population | Recommendation | Schedule |
|------------|---------------|----------|
| Routine | Age 11-12 years (may start at age 9) | 2-dose series if starting before 15th birthday (0, 6-12 months) |
| Catch-up | Ages 13-26 years | 3-dose series (0, 1-2 months, 6 months) |
| Adults 27-45 | **Shared clinical decision-making** | 3-dose series if electing vaccination |
| Immunocompromised (including HIV) | Recommended through age 26; 3-dose series even if initiated at age 9-14 [^274^] |

### Key Clinical Points
- Vaccination not recommended during pregnancy; no intervention needed if inadvertently administered
- No pregnancy test needed before vaccination
- HPV vaccination for all eligible persons regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity
- Target population for adults 27-45: those most likely to benefit (new sexual partners, not previously infected with vaccine types)

---

## 1.6 Pneumococcal Vaccines

### Overview
Pneumococcal disease remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality, particularly in older adults and those with certain medical conditions. The 2024-2025 schedule includes four pneumococcal vaccines: PCV15, PCV20, PCV21, and PPSV23. [^461^] [^462^] [^467^]

### Available Vaccines

| Vaccine | Valency | Indications |
|---------|---------|-------------|
| PCV15 (VAXNEUVANCE) | 15-valent conjugate | Adults 19+ with risk conditions |
| PCV20 (Prevnar 20) | 20-valent conjugate | Adults 50+; one-and-done option |
| PCV21 (CAPVAXIVE) | 21-valent conjugate | Adults 50+; one-and-done option [^467^] |
| PPSV23 (Pneumovax 23) | 23-valent polysaccharide | Follows PCV15 when sequential approach used |

### Adult Recommendations

| Population | Recommendation |
|------------|---------------|
| Adults 50+ (never received PCV) | Single dose of PCV15, PCV20, or PCV21. If PCV15 used: follow with PPSV23 at >=1 year (>=8 weeks if immunocompromised, CSF leak, or cochlear implant). If PCV20 or PCV21: no additional vaccine needed [^467^] |
| Adults 19-49 with risk conditions | Single dose of PCV15, PCV20, or PCV21; risk conditions include: chronic heart/lung/liver disease, diabetes, cigarette smoking, alcoholism, immunocompromising conditions, CSF leak, cochlear implant |
| Adults 65+ with prior PCV13 and PPSV23 | Shared clinical decision-making regarding PCV20 or PCV21 (single dose, at least 5 years after last pneumococcal vaccine) [^461^] |

### Clinical Tool
The CDC offers the **PneumoRecs VaxAdvisor** mobile app for patient-specific pneumococcal vaccine guidance. [^462^]

---

## 1.7 Shingles (Herpes Zoster) Vaccine

### Overview
Herpes zoster (shingles) affects approximately 1 in 3 adults in their lifetime, with risk increasing dramatically with age. Postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) is the most common complication and can cause debilitating chronic pain.

### Recommendations

| Population | Vaccine | Schedule | Efficacy |
|------------|---------|----------|----------|
| All adults 50+ | RZV (Shingrix) | 2 doses, 2-6 months apart | 97% (ages 50-69); 91% (ages 70+) [^465^] |
| Adults 19+ with immunocompromising conditions | RZV (Shingrix) | 2 doses, 1-2 months apart (may extend to 2-6 months if needed) | High efficacy across immunocompromised groups |

### Key Clinical Points
- **No maximum age** for vaccination [^465^]
- Efficacy against PHN: 91% (ages 50+), 89% (ages 70+)
- Should vaccinate even if previously had shingles, received Zostavax, or received varicella vaccine
- No specific waiting period after shingles episode; vaccinate after rash resolves
- Contraindicated during current episode of herpes zoster and during pregnancy
- Common adverse effects: injection site pain (78%), fatigue (46%), myalgia (45%), headache (38%), fever (18%) -- typically resolve within 2-3 days [^465^]
- Very rare risk of Guillain-Barre syndrome reported

---

## 1.8 Hepatitis A and B Vaccines

### Hepatitis A
- **2-dose series** for adults at risk [^518^]
- Risk groups: travelers to endemic areas, men who have sex with men (MSM), persons who use drugs, persons with chronic liver disease
- Combined HepA-HepB vaccine (Twinrix) available: 3-dose series (0, 1, 6 months)

### Hepatitis B (Updated Universal Recommendation)

**2022-2023 ACIP Update:** All adults aged 19-59 years should receive routine HepB vaccination. This replaces the previous risk-based approach to improve coverage. [^519^] [^523^]

| Population | Recommendation |
|------------|---------------|
| Adults 19-59 years | **Universal vaccination** (catch-up if not previously vaccinated) [^523^] |
| Adults 60+ with risk factors | Recommended |
| Adults 60+ without risk factors | May receive vaccine if desired |

### Hepatitis B Vaccine Options

| Vaccine | Schedule | Notes |
|---------|----------|-------|
| Heplisav-B | 2 doses, 1 month apart | Adults 18+; enhanced immunogenicity |
| Engerix-B | 3 doses (0, 1, 6 months) | Standard option |
| Recombivax HB | 3 doses (0, 1, 6 months) | Standard option |
| Twinrix (HepA+HepB) | 3 doses (0, 1, 6 months) | For those needing both |

### Risk Factors for Adults 60+
- Sexual exposure risks (MSM, multiple partners, STI evaluation)
- Percutaneous/mucosal blood exposure (injection drug use, healthcare workers, dialysis)
- HIV, hepatitis C, chronic liver disease
- Travel to endemic countries, diabetes
- Incarcerated persons [^523^]

### Universal Hepatitis B Screening (2023)
All adults 18+ should be screened at least once with a **triple panel**: HBsAg, anti-HBs, total anti-HBc. Pregnant people should be tested during each pregnancy. [^517^]

---

## 1.9 MMR and Varicella Vaccines

### MMR (Measles, Mumps, Rubella)

**Evidence of Immunity (at least one of the following):** [^274^] [^541^]
- Documentation of adequate vaccination (2 doses measles/mumps, 1 dose rubella; doses separated by >=28 days)
- Laboratory evidence of immunity
- Laboratory confirmation of disease
- Birth before 1957 (except healthcare personnel)

| Population | Recommendation |
|------------|---------------|
| Adults without evidence of immunity | 1 dose MMR |
| Healthcare personnel, students, travelers without evidence | 2 doses MMR [^274^] |
| Healthcare personnel born 1957+ | Documentation of 2 doses MMR or lab evidence of immunity [^536^] |
| Pregnancy | MMR **contraindicated**; give 1 dose postpartum before discharge if no rubella immunity [^274^] |

### Varicella (Chickenpox)

**Evidence of Immunity:** [^533^] [^540^]
- Documentation of 2 doses of varicella vaccine
- Laboratory evidence of immunity
- Birth in US before 1980 (not for HCP, pregnant women, immunocompromised)
- Diagnosis/verification of varicella or shingles by healthcare provider

| Population | Recommendation |
|------------|---------------|
| Healthcare personnel without evidence of immunity | 2 doses, 4-8 weeks apart [^536^] |
| Adults without evidence of immunity | 2 doses, 4-8 weeks apart |

### Key Clinical Points
- 70-90% of adults who do not remember having varicella actually have antibodies [^540^]
- Serologic testing before vaccination may be cost-effective in adults with uncertain history
- MMR and varicella can be given simultaneously; if not given on same day, separate by at least 28 days

---

## 1.10 RSV (Respiratory Syncytial Virus) Vaccine

### Overview
RSV causes significant respiratory disease in older adults, with an estimated 60,000-160,000 hospitalizations and 6,000-10,000 deaths annually among adults 65+ in the United States. [^452^] [^515^]

### 2024 Updated Recommendations

| Population | Recommendation |
|------------|---------------|
| Adults 75+ years | RSV vaccination **recommended** (routine) [^452^] |
| Adults 60-74 years at **increased risk** | RSV vaccination recommended for those with: chronic cardiopulmonary disease, diabetes, moderate/severe immune compromise, chronic kidney/liver/hematologic disorders, neurologic/neuromuscular conditions, nursing home residents, frailty [^530^] |
| Pregnancy | RSV vaccination (Abrysvo) at **32-36 weeks gestation** during RSV season [^542^] |

### Available Vaccines
- **Abrysvo** (Pfizer) -- single dose
- **Arexvy** (GSK) -- single dose
- **mResvia** (Moderna) -- single dose [^452^]

### Key Clinical Points
- **Single dose only**; no repeat dosing currently recommended
- Coadministration with other vaccines (influenza, COVID-19) acceptable [^515^]
- Common adverse effects: injection site pain, fatigue, headache, myalgia
- Rare safety signal: potential association with Guillain-Barre syndrome (under investigation)

---

| Vaccine | 19-26 | 27-49 | 50-64 | 65+ | Special Populations |
